newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Ares-Serono sees continued 97 profit rise.
newsitem.headline: Ares-Serono sees continued 97 profit rise.

text.p: Pharmaceuticals group Ares-Serono's 1997 sales and profits are expected to grow at rates seen in the first half and dividends should rise along with profits, finance chief Jacques Theurillat said.
First-half sales for Ares-Serono, a leader in infertility treatment, rose 16.4 percent to $437.6 million, while net income nearly doubled to 41.1 million.
The third quarter is traditionally weak as couples seeking fertility treatment go on holiday, he told Reuters in an interview.
"We will have a strong fourth quarter, as almost always has been the case in the past," he added.
"In the end, I think we will have, referring to the financial year, more or less the same trend as we saw in the first six months." He declined to elaborate.
Rising profits could boost dividends on 1997 results as well, Theurillat said, noting the biotechnology company intended to keep its payout ratio at around 25 percent.

"We will try to follow a constant dividend policy. We are trying to reward shareholders properly. The fact that last year we doubled the dividend compared with an 81 percent increase in net income means we are trying to reward the shareholder for his support," he said.
It is up to shareholders to vote on dividends, he said, but added: "If we increase our net income, I think it is fair to reward shareholders who have been with us during this period."
Ares-Serono boosted its dividend on 1996 results to five Swiss francs per bearer share from three and to two francs per registered share from 1.20.
Group net rose to $53.5 million in 1996 from $29.4 million on sales of $805.0 million, up from $682.3 million.
He said the company was on track to boost its operating margin to 20 percent in the next two to three years from around 12 percent last year and 17 percent in the first half of 1997.
Theurillat also said Ares-Serono was on the lookout for acquisitions and joint ventures that could boost its product pipeline and fuel growth that has traditionally come from within.
"In the next one to two years you will see a lot of activity on our side in mergers and acquisitions," he said, adding purchasing even a large company was conceivable if the opportunity arose.
The company will stick to its core businesses, he said. It was also considering ways to reduce its risks by moving some of its research and development business off its own balance sheet.

He said the company's price/earnings ratio was higher than that of U.S. biotech companies but said this was justified given its strong product pipeline, its international strength and its robust product launch schedule.
